exercises.heading: 9.7 Section Exercises
Verbal

problem.paragraph: What term is used to express the likelihood of an event occurring? Are there restrictions on its values? If so, what are they? If not, explain.

solution.paragraph: probability; The probability of an event is restricted to values between $$0 0$$ and $$1, 1,$$ inclusive of $$0 0$$ and $$1. 1.$$

problem.paragraph: What is a sample space?
What is an experiment?

solution.paragraph: An experiment is an activity with an observable result.

problem.paragraph: What is the difference between events and outcomes? Give an example of both using the sample space of tossing a coin 50 times.

The union of two sets is defined as a set of elements that are present in at least one of the sets. How is this similar to the definition used for the union of two events from a probability model? How is it different?

solution.paragraph: The probability of the union of two events occurring is a number that describes the likelihood that at least one of the events from a probability model occurs. In both a union of sets $$A and B A and B$$ and a union of events $$A and B, A and B,$$ the union includes either $$A or B A or B$$ or both. The difference is that a union of sets results in another set, while the union of events is a probability, so it is always a numerical value between $$0 0$$ and $$1. 1.$$

exercises.paragraph: For the following exercises, two coins are tossed.

problem.paragraph: What is the sample space?
Find the probability of tossing two heads.
Find the probability of tossing exactly one tail.
Find the probability of tossing at least one tail.

exercises.paragraph: For the following exercises, four coins are tossed.

problem.paragraph: What is the sample space?
Find the probability of tossing exactly two heads.
Find the probability of tossing exactly three heads.
Find the probability of tossing four heads or four tails.
Find the probability of tossing all tails.
Find the probability of tossing not all tails.
Find the probability of tossing exactly two heads or at least two tails.
Find the probability of tossing either two heads or three heads.

exercises.paragraph: For the following exercises, use this scenario: a bag of M&Ms contains $$6$$ blue, $$10$$ brown, $$8$$ orange, $$8$$ yellow, $$4$$ red, and $$4$$ green M&Ms. Reaching into the bag, a person grabs 5 M&Ms.

problem.paragraph: What is the probability of getting all blue M&Ms?
What is the probability of getting $$3$$ blue M&Ms?
What is the probability of getting $$20$$ blue M&Ms?
What is the probability of getting no brown M&Ms?

exercises.heading: Extensions
exercises.paragraph: Use the following scenario for the exercises that follow: In the game of Keno, a player starts by selecting $$1$$ numbers from the numbers $$80.$$ to $$20$$ After the player makes his selections, $$1$$ winning numbers are randomly selected from numbers $$80.$$ to $$3,4,$$ A win occurs if the player has correctly selected $$5$$ or $$20$$ of the $$20 20$$ winning numbers. (Round all answers to the nearest hundredth of a percent.)

problem.paragraph: What is the percent chance that a player selects exactly 3 winning numbers?
What is the percent chance that a player selects exactly 4 winning numbers?
What is the percent chance that a player selects all 5 winning numbers?
What is the percent chance of winning?
How much less is a player’s chance of selecting 3 winning numbers than the chance of selecting either 4 or 5 winning numbers?

exercises.heading: Real-World Applications
exercises.paragraph: Use this data for the exercises that follow: In 2013, there were roughly 317 million citizens in the United States, and about 40 million were elderly (aged 65 and over).2

problem.paragraph: If you meet a U.S. citizen, what is the percent chance that the person is elderly? (Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.)
If you meet five U.S. citizens, what is the percent chance that exactly one is elderly? (Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.)
If you meet five U.S. citizens, what is the percent chance that three are elderly? (Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.)
If you meet five U.S. citizens, what is the percent chance that four are elderly? (Round to the nearest thousandth of a percent.)

It is predicted that by 2030, one in five U.S. citizens will be elderly. How much greater will the chances of meeting an elderly person be at that time? What policy changes do you foresee if these statistics hold true?
